<x_0.0693><y_0.0>Pole. Ankudinoff’s veffel was wrecked, and the crew ditru-
buted among the other two. Soon after this the two
veffels loft right of each other, and never joined again.
Delhneff was driven about by tempelluous winds till
October, when he was flipwrecked confidarably to the
fourth of the Andyr. Having at last reached that ri-
ver, he formed a fcheme of returning by the fame way
that he had come, but never made the attempt. As
for Alexeeff, after being alfo hipwrecked, he had died
of the fourvy, together with Ankudinoff; part of the
crew were killed by the favages, and a few escaped to
Kamfehatka, where they fettled."<x_0.9717><y_0.1625><class_Text>

<x_0.2168><y_0.1547>From Captain * Cook's voyage towards the north-
eaftern parts of Afia, it appears that it is polible to
double the promontory of Tichutki without any great
difficulty: and it now appears, that the continents of
Afia and America are feparated from one another but
by a narrow fitait, which is free from ice; but, to the
northwards, that experienced navigator was everywhere
topped by the ice in the month of Augufl, fo that he
could neither trace the American continent farther than
to the latitude of 70°, nor reach the mouth of the river
Kovyma on the Afiatic continent; though it is pro-
bable that this might have been done at another time,
when the situation of the ice was altered either by winds
or currents.<x_0.9766><y_0.3477><class_Text>

<x_0.2285><y_0.3406>On the whole, therefore, it appears that the infur-
mountable obtacle in the north-caft pallage lies between
the rivers Pialda and Chatanga ; and unlefs there be in
that space a connection between the Afiatic and Amer-
rican continents, there is not in any other part. Ice,
however, is as effectual an obtfruction as land : and
though the voyage were to be made by accident for
once, it never could be efteemed a pallage calculated
for the purposes of trade, or any other beneficial pur-
pode whatever.<x_0.9844><y_0.4813><class_Text>

<x_0.0928><y_0.4766>Of the
north-weft
pallage.<x_0.2256><y_0.5234><class_Caption>

<x_0.2344><y_0.4734>With regard to the north-weft paffage, the fame dif-
ficulties occur as in the other. Captain Cook's voyage
has now affirmed us, that if there is any fitait which di-
vides the continent of America into two, it mull lie in
a higher latitude than 70°, and consequently be perpe-
tually frozen up. If a north-weft paffage can be found
then, it mull be by failing round the whole American
continent, instead of feeking a pallage through it, which
fome have supposed to exit at the bottom of Baffin's
bay. But the extent of the American continent to the
northward is yet unknown; and there is a polibility of
its being joined to that part of Afia between the Pialda
and Chatanga, which has never yet been circumnaviga-
ted . It remains therefore to confer, whether there
is any polibility of attaining the wilhed-for pallage by
failing directly north, between the eastern and weftern
continents.<x_0.999><y_0.7047><class_Text>

<x_0.2412><y_0.6992>Of the practicability of this method, the Honourable
Daines Barrington is very confident, as appears by fe-
veral tracts which he published in the years 1773 and
1776, in consequence of the unfucceful attempts
made by Captain Phipps, now Lord Mulgrave. See
_Noarm-Keft Paffage._— In the tracts now alluded to

reached very high northern latitudes; may, fome who
